narrative:
The model determined that you have an 82% chance of failing the bar exam on your first attempt. Because this predicted risk is so high, the law school decided to reject your application.

Three factors drove this outcome, ranked by importance. Your first-year and third-year class rankings were the strongest influence. Standing in the bottom decile both times, far below the average of roughly sixth decile among accepted students, signaled to the model that you would likely struggle with the demands of law school and the bar exam. This pushed the prediction heavily toward failure.

Your LSAT score of 22.5 was the second most important factor. It sits well below the 37-point average of admitted students and strongly reinforced the likelihood of not passing the bar.

Your undergraduate GPA of 2.7 worked in the opposite direction. Although it is noticeably lower than the 3.23 average of accepted applicants, the model still viewed it as a mildly positive signal compared with the rest of your record.

Taken together, the combination of persistently low class rank and a low LSAT score outweighed the modest positive effect of your college grades, leading to the rejection.

You should focus on raising your LSAT score through intensive preparation, consider repeating key courses to improve your academic standing, and then reapply. Many students successfully turn around similar profiles with targeted improvement.
